questions.question_text:
A credit card charges $14.6\%$ p.a. compounded daily.
A purchase is made on $9$ July and the statement is issued on $31$ July, with interest charged from and including the purchase date to and including the statement date.
What is the daily interest rate, and for how many days is interest charged?

options.why: Computed $31 - 9 = 22$ and forgot that the purchase date itself is included, losing one day.
Divided the annual rate by $12$ months instead of $365$ days: $0.146 \div 12 = 0.0122$, which is a monthly rate, not a daily one.
Made both slips at once: divided $0.146$ by $12$ rather than $365$, and used $31 - 9 = 22$ without including the purchase date.

questions.solution_text:
$r = \dfrac{0.146}{365}$
$= 0.0004$ per day
Number of days $= 31 - 9 + 1$
$= 23$ days

questions.question_text:
A purchase of $\$380$ is made on a credit card with no interest-free period charging $21.9\%$ p.a. compounded daily.
Interest is charged for $16$ days.
What is the amount owing, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Gave the interest charged rather than the total amount owing.
Treated the $16$ days as $16$ monthly periods at $\dfrac{0.219}{12}$ each.
Assumed an interest-free period applies, but this card has none.

questions.question_text:
A credit card charges $18.25\%$ p.a. compounded daily with no interest-free period, from and including the purchase date to and including the statement date of $30$ September.
A purchase of $\$600$ is made on $11$ September and one of $\$200$ on $21$ September.
What is the closing balance, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Added the two purchases and charged no interest at all.
Gave the interest charged instead of the closing balance.
Charged $20$ days of interest on both purchases instead of $10$ days on the second.

questions.question_text:
A credit card charges $25.55\%$ p.a. compounded daily.
A single purchase of $\$1800$ is made and interest is charged for $18$ days.
How much interest is charged, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Gave the total amount owing rather than the interest part of it.
Used simple interest for $18$ days instead of daily compounding.
Charged a full year's interest, $1800 \times 0.2555$, instead of $18$ days.

questions.question_text:
A credit card statement shows a closing balance of $\$1740.80$.
The minimum payment is $3\%$ of the closing balance.
What is the minimum payment, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Gave the whole closing balance instead of the small percentage required.
Took $1\%$ of the closing balance instead of $3\%$.
Divided the closing balance by $30$ instead of multiplying by $0.03$.

questions.question_text:
Tom's credit card has a $55$-day interest-free period that applies only when the previous statement was paid in full.
Last month Tom paid only the minimum payment.
He then buys a $\$900$ laptop $30$ days before his next statement.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: Interest is charged on the $\$900$ from the purchase date, because the interest-free period does not apply this month.
No interest is charged, because $30$ days is inside the $55$-day interest-free period.
options.why: The interest-free period is not available at all when the previous statement was not paid in full.

options.text: No interest is charged, because Tom made a minimum payment last month.
options.why: A minimum payment is not payment in full, which is what the interest-free period requires.

options.text: Interest is charged only on the days after the first $55$ days from the purchase.
options.why: When no interest-free period applies, interest runs from the purchase date, not from day $56$.

questions.solution_text:
The interest-free period applies only when the previous statement was paid in full.
Tom paid only the minimum, so it does not apply this month.
Interest is therefore charged on the $\$900$ from and including the purchase date.

questions.question_text:
Nadia owes $\$1450$ on a credit card charging $18.25\%$ p.a. compounded daily.
Interest is charged for $25$ days, after which she repays $\$600$.
How much does she owe immediately after the repayment, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Subtracted the repayment but charged no interest for the $25$ days.
Gave the balance before the repayment was subtracted.
Gave the interest charged over the $25$ days rather than the amount still owing.

questions.question_text: Why is a credit card described as a reducing balance loan?

options.text: Interest is charged on the amount currently owing, which falls each time a repayment is made.
Interest is charged on the original amount spent, so the total is fixed from the start.
options.why: That describes a flat-rate loan; a reducing balance loan charges interest on the current balance.

options.text: The interest rate itself is reduced a little each month that the card is used.
options.why: It is the balance that reduces, not the interest rate, which stays the same.

options.text: The minimum payment reduces each month, so the debt is guaranteed to be cleared.
options.why: A falling minimum payment does not clear the debt; interest still accrues on what is left.

questions.solution_text:
Interest on a credit card is worked out on the amount currently owing, not on the amount first spent.
Each repayment lowers that balance, so the next interest charge is smaller.
That is exactly how a reducing balance loan behaves.
